label: Two-week sprint
summary: A two-week sprint is a fixed time-box borrowed from IT scrum, where it originated as a natural fit for developing, testing and deploying software features. Maaike questions whether this period maps onto the actual content creation and publication cycle of conversational teams. The two-week sprint is treated as a default that organisations often copy uncritically rather than one that was ever designed for content work.
how_maaike_uses: Maaike uses the two-week sprint as a contrast case to argue that conversational teams should examine whether their own publication and research cycles actually fit a two-week rhythm before adopting it. Drawing on her experience as a tech writer in aviation, where a four-week cycle with a fixed monthly publication window felt natural, she points out that blindly applying the IT default can create artificial deadlines and a rules-for-rules-sake attitude. Her angle is empirical: sprint length should reflect the real effort cycle of the team, not an inherited convention.
open_questions: What sprint length would actually fit most conversational or chatbot teams if not two weeks?
How should teams go about measuring whether their chosen sprint length is working, given the Agile emphasis on empirical and objectively measurable performance?
